title: Meta ran ads for an app promising to nudify female politicians
gist: Meta ran video ads for the AI porn app Kromix depicting a deepfaked politician, despite explicit rules against sexual ad content, part of a broader pattern of Meta removing hundreds of thousands of nudify-app ads after journalists flagged them rather than catching them proactively.

insights.claim: Meta ran video ads for an AI porn-generation app called Kromix that depicted a deepfaked video resembling a real female US politician performing in pornography, despite Meta's explicit policy banning ads with sexual content and nonconsensual intimate imagery.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of ad-review failure at Meta on a high-risk content category involving political deepfakes, a recurring regulatory and reputational liability.
insights.quote: no restrictions... all the characters are real people... the AI that men actually use
insights.locator: A voice-over for one of the video advertisements

insights.claim: The Kromix ad account was created on August 3, 2026, had zero followers, and ran 32 ads for between 5 and 46 hours before removal, suggesting Meta's automated ad-review system does not flag basic risk signals like brand-new, follower-less accounts.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A documented technical failure mode relevant to assessing Meta's claims about the reliability of its AI-driven ad review.
insights.locator: The page running the advertisements was created on August 3

insights.claim: Meta removed over 340,000 ads for nudify apps between November 2025 and January 2026 alone, by its own count, indicating the scale of ongoing enforcement failures and prevalence of nudify advertisers on the platform despite active removal efforts.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of an unresolved content-moderation cost center that could invite regulatory fines under frameworks like the EU DSA or state AG actions as scrutiny grows.
insights.quote: removing over 340,000 violating ads for nudify apps late last year alone
insights.locator: Cindy Southworth, head of women's safety at Meta

insights.claim: Meta has separately removed CSAM-adjacent ads -- including apps face-swapping children into sexual content -- that ran between November 2025 and August 2026 and sometimes reached thousands of people across the US, UK, and a dozen-plus European countries, even after Meta said it had deployed new upload-time AI detection.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Undercuts Meta's public claims about the effectiveness of its AI-based ad moderation, a factor for reputational-risk investors and regulators evaluating platform liability.
insights.locator: researchers had stumbled across more than 50 ads on Meta's platforms

themes.theme: Deepfake harms spreading via mainstream AI

insights.claim: Officials in Sweden, England, and Northern Ireland were targeted with sexualized deepfakes made using Grok in January 2026, and roughly 3 million sexualized images of women and girls were created using Grok around the same period.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Indicates nudify and deepfake harms are already spreading via mainstream, well-funded AI tools rather than only fringe apps like Kromix, broadening the regulatory exposure beyond niche developers.
insights.locator: as Grok was used to create around 3 million sexualized images

insights.claim: Both Apple's App Store and Meta's ad platform have repeatedly hosted and then removed nudify apps (Kromix, MaskAI) only after journalists contacted the companies, indicating press and researcher scrutiny -- not proactive platform enforcement -- is currently the primary check on this content category.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Suggests continued reputational and legal tail risk for platforms until proactive detection improves, and an opportunity for third-party trust-and-safety tooling vendors.
insights.locator: App Store after WIRED contacted Apple for comment

insights.claim: Researcher Katie Paul of the Tech Transparency Project attributes the ad-moderation enforcement gap partly to Meta increasingly relying on AI moderation while laying off human moderators.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Ties specific staffing/automation decisions to observed moderation failures, a relevant operational risk factor for Meta's ad business.
insights.quote: Ads are Meta's primary product, and there appears to be zero quality control. Meta is also making a lot of statements publicly, banking on their AI and the sophistication of it, while simultaneously saying they use AI to review their ad library and nothing's perfect.
